title: Is this risk approach appropriate?
blurb: Judge whether risk is being managed well in an agile scenario, including how the Agilometer is used, and pick the reason that explains it.
question: Saltmarsh's project manager fills in the Agilometer herself the night before the project initiation workshop and presents it as the project's view. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?

teach.h: Four tests for any risk decision
teach.body: Test a risk decision four ways. Rhythm: are risks identified in every planning session and retrospective, with responses implemented and communicated inside the iterations? Tool: is each artifact used for its own job? Agilometer: is it assessed by all participants, combined, revisited regularly and acted on slider by slider? Tracking: are responses prioritized with the work and is total exposure kept up to date? A 'No' usually breaks one of these.

root.label: A risk decision in the scenario

teach.h: Fit for purpose or poor fit?

rows.label: Agilometer input
values: The PM's view on its own

teach.caption: 10.3.1, 10.3.2, 10.4.2, Tables 13.5 and 13.7.

head: Low slider
An action that fits
rows: Challenge whether too many items are Must haves, or the assumptions behind them
Use contracts that support agile, such as fixed teams and cost per iteration
Arrange co-location or remote tools that support transparency and rich communication
Ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally
Plan frequent releases so benefit arrives in regular partial deliveries
teach.caption: 10.3.2.3 for flexibility; the other actions draw on the commercial management approach and team structure (Table 7.3) and the benefits approach (Table 6.1).

teach.body: The Agilometer identifies and monitors the risks of agile working. Treat these as warning signs: using it to accept or reject a change request (that is the issues practice); using it as a progress measure; one person scoring it for everyone; assessing it once and never again; or noting a low slider without doing anything about it. Each breaks how the risk practice intends the tool to be used.

teach.h: A risk burn-down kept current, or not
teach.caption: A flat line can simply mean nobody has revisited the likelihoods. The technique expects an update at every planning session (10.4.2).

teach.body: In the project initiation workshop, the service design team, digital team, Coastline and the tenants' panel each score the Agilometer anonymously, and project manager Sally Greaves combines the scores. Environmental conditions is low because Coastline is paid per job and must agree any change to how engineers work, so she logs the threat in the risk register. At the agile enablement workshop, staff fears about job losses are raised under risk identification. Response stories join the risk-adjusted product backlog.

steps.label: Reason
steps.sub: Choose the one that explains this case

teach.text: Traps: 'the board reviews the Agilometer in agile enablement' is true but does not make it a tool for deciding change requests. 'Must haves are fixed' is true, yet challenging whether an item really is a Must have is exactly how the flexibility slider is raised. 'Stage boundaries confirm risks are acceptable' is true but does not justify pausing risk identification between them.

items: Fit for purpose = identified each planning and retro, right tool, Agilometer used as intended, kept current.
The Agilometer is assessed by all participants and combined, then reassessed regularly.
A low slider calls for action on that area, such as challenging Must haves for flexibility.
The Agilometer assesses agile-working risk; it does not decide change requests or show progress.
Update risk likelihoods at each planning session so the risk burn-down tells the truth.

summary: You can now judge whether risk management in an agile scenario is fit for purpose, from the rhythm of identification to the use of the Agilometer, the risk-adjusted backlog and the cumulative risk burn-down. You can also choose the reason that explains the verdict rather than a true but irrelevant one.

A.q: Callowmere University's Student Support Hub project is in initiation. The evening before the project initiation workshop, project manager Jamal Hussain completes the Agilometer on his own, then presents it in the workshop as the project's assessment. What should happen instead?
options: The board completes it at the first progress review
The agile coach completes it during project closure
All participants assess it and the scores are combined
The team coach completes a new one for every sprint
A.why: In the project initiation workshop all participants assess the Agilometer, anonymously or in groups, and the results are combined into one project Agilometer (Table 13.7, 10.3.2).

whyNot.0: The progress review looks at stage status; the Agilometer is first assessed by all participants in the project initiation workshop.
whyNot.1: Agilometer trends feed closure lessons, but the assessment is needed at the start and regularly afterwards.
whyNot.3: The Agilometer is a project-level risk tool reassessed in agile enablement workshops, not a per-sprint team form.

A.q: Larkspur Rail's app team identifies risks in every sprint planning session. It proposes recording each agreed risk response as a story in its product backlog, so that the responses are prioritized alongside the feature stories. How well does this apply the risk practice, and why?
options: Well, because responses are prioritized with the stories
Well, because it removes the need for a risk register
Poorly, because responses belong in the risk approach
Poorly, because responses are planned at stage boundaries
A.why: A risk-adjusted product backlog holds stories and risk responses together, so responses are prioritized and delivered within the iterations (10.4.1).

whyNot.1: The risk register still records the risks and their status; the backlog holds the responses as work.
whyNot.2: The risk management approach describes how risk is managed; it does not hold the responses to be prioritized.
whyNot.3: Responses are planned and implemented within the iteration cycles, not saved up for stage boundaries.

A.q: Easterholm County Council's digital team set a likelihood for each tracked risk at its first planning meeting and drew a cumulative risk burn-down chart. Five sprints later the line is flat because the likelihoods have not been looked at since. What should change?
options: Plot the story points remaining on the chart instead
Update each likelihood at every planning session
Pass the chart to the board to keep until closure
Track the same risks on a cumulative flow diagram
A.why: The team defines each risk's likelihood at the first planning meeting and updates it at every following planning session, so the chart shows true total exposure (10.4.2).

whyNot.0: Story points remaining belong on a burn-down chart of work; this chart tracks risk exposure.
whyNot.2: The chart is the team's working tool, updated each planning session, not something held by the board.
whyNot.3: A cumulative flow diagram shows workflow states and bottlenecks, not risk exposure.

B.q: At Saltmarsh Housing Group's agile enablement workshop, contact centre staff raise a fear that online reporting will lead to job losses and slow the adoption of the new ways of working. This threat is not covered by any Agilometer slider and has not been raised before. Under which workshop topic should it be discussed FIRST?
options: Agilometer assessment review
Risk assessment
Risk planning
Risk identification
B.why: The agile enablement workshop's risk identification topic covers extra threats and opportunities to agile adoption that the Agilometer does not capture (Table 13.5).

whyNot.0: The Agilometer assessment review links the existing slider results to agile values and objectives; this threat is outside the sliders.
whyNot.1: Risk assessment estimates probability and impact once a risk has been identified.
whyNot.2: Risk planning agrees practical responses after the risk has been identified and assessed.

B.q: Larkspur Rail's head of customer relations raised the threat that automatic payment could increase fraud. The team assessed it and agreed a response story for extra fraud checks. During sprint 5, the Coinbridge team builds that story as part of its normal sprint work. Which risk step is now taking place?
options: Implement
Plan
Assess
Communicate
B.why: Implementing responses is part of the continuous iteration cycles in PRINCE2 Agile (10.3.1).

whyNot.1: The response was planned when the story was agreed; building it is implementation.
whyNot.2: Assessment estimated and evaluated the threat earlier; it is not what is happening now.
whyNot.3: Communication runs through feedback loops; the team is carrying out the response.

B.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's head of internal audit asks where he can see every risk identified on the click and collect project, with its current status and how it has changed over time. Where should she look?
options: The risk management approach
The risk-adjusted product backlog
The risk register
The project Agilometer
B.why: The risk register is the record of identified risks, with their status and history (Table 10.1).

whyNot.0: The approach describes how risk is managed, not the individual risks and their history.
whyNot.1: The risk-adjusted backlog holds response stories alongside features, not the full record of each risk.
whyNot.3: The Agilometer rates six areas of agile suitability, not each identified risk.

C.q: In Saltmarsh Housing Group's project initiation workshop, the service design team, the digital team, Coastline and members of the tenants' panel each score the Agilometer anonymously. The project manager combines the scores into one project Agilometer and logs the low environmental conditions score as a threat. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
options: Yes, because all participants assess and the results are combined
Yes, because the Agilometer replaces the risk register
No, because the board should score it in directing a project
No, because suppliers should be kept out of the assessment
C.why: In the project initiation workshop all participants assess the Agilometer, anonymously or in groups, and the scores are combined into one project Agilometer; risks found are recorded in the risk register (Table 13.7, Table 10.1).

whyNot.1: The Agilometer and the risk register are separate artifacts; the threat is rightly logged in the register.
whyNot.2: The board reassesses it in agile enablement, but the first assessment involves all participants in initiation.
whyNot.3: Suppliers are part of the agile delivery, so their view of agile-working risks is valuable.

C.q: Draycott Precision Engineering has never used agile outside its software team. The board completed an Agilometer during initiation, filed it with the PID and has not looked at it since, although the project is now in its third stage. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
options: Yes, because it combined everyone's views in initiation
Yes, because the business case is checked at boundaries
No, because it should be reassessed at regular intervals
No, because the delivery team should own the Agilometer
C.why: The agile enablement workshop provides regular Agilometer assessments in initiation and later stages, so that agile maturity and agile-working risks are monitored (Table 13.5, 10.3.1).

whyNot.0: Combining views in initiation is right, but the tool must also be used to monitor risks as the project goes on.
whyNot.1: Business justification is checked at boundaries, but that does not explain why the Agilometer can be left untouched.
whyNot.3: The board, agile coaches and business representatives reassess it in agile enablement workshops; it is not a team artifact.

C.q: Callowmere University's Agilometer is low on ease of communication, because wellbeing staff work across two campuses and many work part-time or remotely. The project manager arranges a shared online board and short, regular video sessions between the staff and the web team. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
options: Yes, because remote working raises flexibility on delivery
Yes, because it acts on the area the slider shows as weak
No, because communication belongs to the people element
No, because sliders are fixed once initiation has ended
C.why: A low Agilometer slider is a risk to agile working to be acted on; tools and arrangements that support transparent, rich communication between remote staff address ease of communication (10.3.2, Table 7.3).

whyNot.0: Flexibility on what is delivered concerns comfort with flexing scope, not where people work.
whyNot.2: Communication is a people topic too, but improving a low slider is part of managing agile-working risk.
whyNot.3: The Agilometer is reassessed regularly and sliders can and should be improved during the project.

reteach.title: A school trip risk check
reteach.question: A teacher plans a week-long field trip. What separates a sensible approach to risk from a box-ticking one?

blocks.h: Living risk, not a filed form
blocks.body: A sensible teacher asks staff and pupils' helpers what could go wrong, at every evening review, not only before departure. She keeps a log of hazards and actions, and she rates how ready the group is to work in small independent teams. If one rating is low, say the groups find it hard to keep in touch, she fixes that, for example with radios. A box-ticking teacher fills in the form alone, files it and never looks again.

blocks.text: The readiness rating is not used to decide whether to add a museum visit. That is a change, decided another way.

explain.body: Risks are identified in every planning session and retrospective, and responses are implemented and communicated within the iterations, not saved for stage boundaries.

test.q: Easterholm County Council's digital team adds a 'new risks' item to the agenda of every team retrospective, and records what it finds. How well does this apply the risk practice, and why?
options: Well, because retros are a fixed point for identifying risk
Well, because the board reviews risks in each retro
Poorly, because risks are identified at stage boundaries
Poorly, because retrospectives cover lessons not risks
test.why: Identifying risks is a fixed part of every planning session and team or project retrospective (10.3.1).

whyNot.1: The board does not attend team retrospectives; the team identifies the risks itself.
whyNot.2: Waiting for stage boundaries would leave risks unidentified for weeks; identification happens every iteration.
whyNot.3: Retrospectives cover lessons, and they are also a set point for gathering risks in PRINCE2 Agile.

explain.body: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working. Change requests belong to the issues practice; progress belongs to burn charts and dashboards.

test.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's finance director suggests using the Agilometer in each progress review to show the board how much of the release has been delivered. How well does this apply the risk practice?
options: Well, as it is shown on the project dashboard
Well, as it has a slider about delivery
Poorly, as the agile coach should own it
Poorly, as it assesses agile-working risks
test.why: The Agilometer identifies and monitors the risks of agile working; delivery progress is shown by burn charts on the dashboards (10.3.1, 12.4.3).

whyNot.0: Agilometer trends do appear on the project dashboard, but that does not make it a measure of delivery.
whyNot.1: Flexibility on what is delivered is about stakeholders' attitudes, not the amount delivered.
whyNot.2: The Agilometer is assessed by many people, not owned by the agile coach; the problem is using a risk tool to show progress.

explain.body: The Agilometer is assessed by all participants and combined, then revisited regularly in agile enablement workshops. A low slider is acted on.

test.q: Larkspur Rail's Agilometer shows flexibility on what is delivered as low, because the finance director wants a fixed list of all features. The board notes this in its minutes but agrees no action. What is the BEST criticism?
options: The Agilometer should be moved into the issue register
The finance director should be removed from the board
The slider should be averaged with the other five
A low slider calls for action, such as challenging Musts
test.why: A low slider signals a risk to agile working that should be acted on; flexibility can be raised by challenging whether too many requirements are Must haves (10.3.2.3).

whyNot.0: The Agilometer is a risk product; it does not belong in the issue register.
whyNot.1: Removing a board member is not an agile-risk response; working on his attitude to flexing scope is.
whyNot.2: Combining the sliders does not address the specific weakness in flexibility.

explain.body: With the verdict settled, pick the reason that explains why THIS risk action fits or fails. True statements about risk in general are the usual decoys.

test.q: Draycott's software team updates each risk's likelihood at every planning session, and its cumulative risk burn-down has fallen steadily. You judge this appropriate. Which reason BEST explains why?
options: The board approves the release map at each boundary
Risk exposure is kept current across the iterations
Burn-down charts show work left within an iteration
The Agilometer is reassessed in agile enablement
test.why: Updating likelihoods each planning session keeps the cumulative risk burn-down an accurate picture of total exposure across iterations (10.4.2).

whyNot.0: This is true of stage boundaries but does not explain why the risk burn-down practice is good.
whyNot.2: This describes a work burn-down chart, not a risk burn-down.
whyNot.3: This is true but concerns a different tool from the one in the scenario.
